Chapter 5: The Presidency and the Burden of Unpopular Decisions
Imagine stepping into the presidency, just as John Adams did, with a nation that’s young, hopeful, but already deeply divided. On one side, there were people who wanted to draw closer to France. On the other, folks who believed Britain could offer the stability America needed. Political parties—once thought impossible—were suddenly forming, and each camp was absolutely convinced they were right.
Adams found himself right in the middle, trying to guide the country through these rough waters. The challenges? They came fast. France, furious over America’s neutral stance in its war with Britain, started seizing American ships. Members of Adams’s own party began calling for war, eager to show the world how strong this young nation could be.
But Adams wasn’t quick to take the bait. He remembered what war really cost: the lives lost, families forever changed. He believed peace was worth fighting for—even if it was the harder path.
So, against a tide of fierce opposition, Adams sent envoys to France to try to talk things out. The negotiations were painfully slow and filled with setbacks. Then came the XYZ Affair—news that French officials demanded bribes just to start talking. Outrage exploded back home. Suddenly, Adams was under fire from every direction. Some thought he was too weak; others accused him of being reckless. The whole country felt like it was teetering on the edge of war.
Through it all, Adams wasn’t alone. His partnership with Abigail was a constant source of strength. She offered advice, comfort, and helped him weather the storms of public life. Their shared sense of duty, built over years of sacrifice, held them together. Adams saw firsthand how the presidency could test even the strongest relationships—but he also knew that true partnership could survive anything.
As his presidency came to an end, Adams faced defeat from his old friend—and rival—Thomas Jefferson. But here’s something powerful: the transition of power was peaceful. That moment proved just how strong this new republic had become.
Adams headed home, his reputation battered, but his conscience absolutely clear. He made tough decisions, often at great personal cost, always choosing principle over popularity.
If you look back, there’s a lesson that stands out. The true test of leadership isn’t about the easy choices. It’s about doing what’s right—even when almost everyone else disagrees. Adams’s life, filled with sacrifice and conviction, reminds us that building a nation is ongoing work. And when it comes down to it, the real measure of a leader is the courage to stand alone, right when it matters most.
